posts.title: How to Care for Sterling Silver Jewellery at Home
posts.excerpt: Why silver darkens, how to clean it gently with things you already have, and the simple habits that keep your pieces bright for years.
posts.author: House of Jewelux Atelier
posts.authorBio: The design and care team at our Jaipur atelier, writing about the pieces we make and how to live with them.
posts.coverAlt: A halo ring with a white metal band resting on a dark velvet stand

toc.text: Everyday habits that make the biggest difference
Put it on last, take it off first
Keep it out of water and chemicals
How to clean silver at home

posts.html:
Sterling silver is one of the most rewarding metals to own. It has a soft, cool shine that suits everyday wear and festive dressing alike, and it ages gracefully when it is looked after. The good news is that caring for silver does not need special equipment. A few minutes of attention and a handful of good habits are enough to keep most pieces looking the way they did on the day you first wore them.

Why silver changes colour

Sterling silver is an alloy: 92.5 per cent pure silver mixed with a small amount of another metal, usually copper, to make it strong enough to wear. Silver reacts slowly with sulphur compounds in the air, and the result is a thin, dark layer called tarnish. It is not damage and it is not dirt in the usual sense; it is a surface reaction, and it can be removed.

Tarnish appears faster in some conditions than others:

  • humid weather and coastal air
  • contact with perfume, hair spray, lotions and sunscreen
  • rubber bands, some paper and cardboard, and wool, which can release sulphur
  • long periods in an open dish on a dressing table

Silver that is worn often usually tarnishes less than silver that is stored away. The gentle friction of daily wear keeps the surface clean.

Everyday habits that make the biggest difference

Put it on last, take it off first

Make jewellery the final step when you get ready, after perfume, make-up and hair products have dried. In the evening, take it off before you wash your face or apply creams. This single habit prevents most build-up.

Keep it out of water and chemicals

Remove silver before swimming, bathing, cleaning the house or working out. Chlorine in pools and household cleaners can mark the surface, and sweat contains salts that speed up tarnish.

Wipe after wearing

A soft, lint-free cloth is your best tool. A quick wipe after each wear removes skin oils and moisture before they settle. A dedicated silver polishing cloth works well for regular touch-ups, but use it gently and avoid rubbing over stones or plated areas.

How to clean silver at home

For light tarnish, the mildest method is usually the best:

  1. Fill a bowl with lukewarm water and add a few drops of mild, unscented dish soap.
  2. Let the piece rest for a few minutes.
  3. Clean gently with a very soft toothbrush, paying attention to links and settings.
  4. Rinse in clean water and dry completely with a soft cloth.
  5. Let it air-dry for a little longer before you put it away.

Avoid toothpaste and baking-soda pastes. They are abrasive and can leave fine scratches, especially on high-polish surfaces. Avoid dips and strong chemical cleaners unless you know the piece has no stones, pearls, enamel or plating, because these can be dulled or damaged.

Pieces that need extra care

Some jewellery should not be soaked at all. Pearls, opals, emeralds and many treated or porous stones can be harmed by water, heat or chemicals. Pieces with oxidised (deliberately darkened) details also need care, because aggressive cleaning removes the contrast that makes the design stand out. For these, a dry, soft cloth is the safest option, and anything more is best left to a jeweller.

Storing silver properly

Good storage slows tarnish more than anything else:

  • Keep each piece in its own soft pouch or a lined compartment so pieces do not scratch each other.
  • Store in a cool, dry place, away from bathrooms and windows.
  • Add a small anti-tarnish strip or a sachet of silica gel to the box to absorb moisture.
  • Fasten chains before storing them so they do not knot.

If you have a piece you wear only for festivals or weddings, check on it every few months and give it a gentle wipe even if you have not worn it.

When to see a professional

Some situations are better handled at the bench: deep, long-standing tarnish, loose stones, bent prongs, worn clasps or a chain that keeps catching. A jeweller can polish, check settings and repair small issues before they turn into lost stones. Many people have their most-worn pieces checked once a year, which is a sensible habit for rings and bracelets in particular, since they take the most knocks.

A short checklist

  • Jewellery on last, off first.
  • No water, chemicals or exercise while wearing it.
  • Wipe after every wear.
  • Mild soap and a soft brush for cleaning, nothing abrasive.
  • Separate pouches, a dry place, an anti-tarnish strip.

Looked after this way, sterling silver keeps its brightness for a very long time. If you are unsure how to clean a particular piece, ask our concierge and we will be happy to advise.

posts.title: How to Find Your Ring Size at Home
posts.excerpt: Three reliable ways to measure your ring size without visiting a store, the common mistakes to avoid, and what to do when you are buying a ring as a surprise.
posts.author: House of Jewelux Atelier
posts.authorBio: The design and care team at our Jaipur atelier, writing about the pieces we make and how to live with them.
posts.coverAlt: A couple holding hands, one of them wearing a ring

toc.text: Method 1: measure a ring that already fits
Common mistakes with the paper method
Buying a ring as a surprise
Designs that need extra care with sizing

posts.html:
A ring that fits well is one you forget you are wearing. Too tight and it pinches by the end of the day; too loose and it spins, slides off when your hands are cold, or catches on clothes. Getting the size right before you order saves time, avoids resizing and, for some designs, protects the ring itself. Here is how to measure accurately at home.

Before you measure: timing matters

Fingers change size through the day. They are usually smallest in the morning and when you are cold, and largest in the evening, after exercise or in hot weather. For the most accurate result:

  • measure at the end of the day, when your hands are warm
  • avoid measuring right after a workout, a hot shower or a salty meal
  • measure two or three times on different days if you can

Measure the finger you will actually wear the ring on. Your dominant hand is often slightly larger, and the same finger can differ by half a size between hands.

Method 1: measure a ring that already fits

This is the most reliable home method, because it uses a ring you already know is comfortable.

  1. Choose a ring that fits the intended finger well, ideally with a thin, round band.
  2. Place it on a ruler and measure the inside diameter in millimetres, from inner edge to inner edge.
  3. Measure across the widest point, and measure twice.
  4. Compare your number with the size chart in our size guide.

If the ring you are measuring has a very wide band, choose a size slightly larger for a new ring with a narrow band, and the other way round. Wide bands feel tighter than narrow ones of the same size.

Method 2: the paper strip

If you do not have a ring to measure, a strip of paper works well. Thread or string can stretch, so paper is the better choice.

  1. Cut a strip of paper about 1 cm wide and 10 cm long.
  2. Wrap it around the base of your finger, snug but not tight.
  3. Mark the point where the paper overlaps.
  4. Lay it flat and measure from the end to the mark in millimetres. This is your finger's circumference.
  5. Check that the strip can slide over your knuckle; if your knuckle is larger than the base of your finger, use a size between the two measurements.

Common mistakes with the paper method

  • Wrapping too tightly, which gives a size that will feel uncomfortable.
  • Measuring a cold finger in an air-conditioned room.
  • Forgetting the knuckle, so the ring will not go on.
  • Reading the measurement from the wrong edge of the mark.

Method 3: a ring sizer

A plastic or metal ring sizer, the adjustable kind or a set of sizing rings, gives the most consistent results at home. Try the size you think is right, wear it for a few minutes, and make sure it slides over the knuckle with a little resistance and does not spin freely.

Buying a ring as a surprise

Measuring someone else's finger without them knowing is a challenge, but there are good options:

  • Borrow a ring they already wear on the same finger, and measure the inside diameter as in Method 1. Put it back quickly.
  • Press the ring into a bar of soap to make an impression, which a jeweller can measure.
  • Ask a close friend or family member, who may know their size.
  • If you are unsure, choose a slightly larger size. Making a ring smaller is generally simpler than making it larger.

Designs that need extra care with sizing

Some rings are harder or impossible to resize after they are made:

  • eternity and half-eternity bands set with stones all the way round
  • rings with engraving, enamel or patterns along the full band
  • some tension and open-band designs

For these, it is worth measuring twice and, if possible, using a proper sizer. If you are unsure, ask our concierge before you order and we will help you choose.

The comfortable-fit test

When you try a ring on, it should:

  • slide over the knuckle with gentle pressure
  • sit at the base of the finger without leaving a deep mark
  • not spin all the way round when you shake your hand
  • feel the same in the morning and the evening

A good fit makes a ring something you wear every day rather than on special occasions. A few minutes with a ruler or a paper strip is all it takes.

posts.title: Temple Jewellery: The Story Behind South India's Sacred Ornaments
posts.excerpt: Where temple jewellery comes from, the motifs you will see again and again, how it is made, and how to wear it today without losing its sense of ceremony.
posts.author: House of Jewelux Atelier
posts.authorBio: The design and care team at our Jaipur atelier, writing about the pieces we make and how to live with them.
posts.coverAlt: A golden temple-style carving with deity figures inside a carved shrine

toc.text: From the sanctum to the stage

posts.html:
Few styles of Indian jewellery carry as much meaning as temple jewellery. Its name comes from its origins: ornaments created to adorn the deities in the temples of South India. Over centuries the same designs moved from the sanctum to the stage, where classical dancers wore them, and then into family collections and bridal trousseaus. Today temple jewellery is worn far beyond its region of origin, yet it still carries a sense of ceremony that few other styles match.

From the sanctum to the stage

In many South Indian temples, the deities were dressed and adorned for festivals and daily rituals. The jewellery made for them was generous in scale and rich in symbolism, crafted to be seen from a distance in lamp-lit halls. Classical dance traditions such as Bharatanatyam later adopted similar ornaments, because the dancer often portrays deities and stories from the epics. The stage gave these designs a wider audience, and families began to commission them for weddings and celebrations.

Temple jewellery was first made to honour the divine. That origin is still visible in every motif, every curve of the frame and every row of hanging drops.

The motifs you will recognise

Temple jewellery uses a vocabulary of symbols that appear again and again. Once you know them, you will spot them everywhere:

  • Lakshmi, the goddess of prosperity, often seated on a lotus at the centre of a pendant
  • Lotus flowers, standing for purity and new beginnings
  • Peacocks, associated with grace and beauty and with several deities
  • Mango or paisley shapes, a symbol of fertility and abundance
  • Temple towers and arches, echoing the architecture of the shrines themselves
  • Coin designs, a reminder of prosperity and of old trade routes

Many pieces combine several motifs, with a deity framed by an arch, flanked by peacocks and finished with a fringe of small drops.

How temple jewellery is made

Repoussé and nakshi work

Much of the detail in temple jewellery is raised from sheet metal. In repoussé, the craftsperson works the metal from the back to push the design forward, then refines it from the front. Nakshi work, often used for figurative panels, involves chasing and carving fine details by hand so that faces, garments and flowers stand out in relief. It is slow work, and the depth of the relief is one of the clearest signs of a skilled hand.

Stones and finishing

Traditional pieces were often set with rubies and emeralds, or with coloured stones chosen for their deep red and green tones. Pearls are used in drops and borders. The finish is usually a warm, slightly antique gold tone that suits the figurative details and photographs beautifully under warm light.

The key pieces

A full temple set can include many ornaments, but these are the ones you will see most often:

  1. Haaram: a long necklace, often with a large central pendant.
  2. Kasu mala: a necklace made of rows of coin motifs.
  3. Choker or addigai: a short, close-fitting necklace.
  4. Jhumkas: bell-shaped earrings, often with pearl or stone drops.
  5. Vanki: an armlet shaped to sit on the upper arm.
  6. Oddiyanam: a waist belt, especially in bridal sets.
  7. Nethi chutti: an ornament worn along the hair parting and on the forehead.

Wearing temple jewellery today

Temple jewellery no longer has to mean a full bridal set. Modern ways to wear it include:

  • a single statement pendant on a simple chain with a plain silk or cotton saree
  • temple jhumkas with a contemporary dress or kurta
  • a choker layered with a delicate longer chain
  • a coin necklace as the one ornate piece in an otherwise minimal look

Let one piece lead. Because the designs are so detailed, a single ornament often says more than a full set.

Caring for temple pieces

The raised details that make temple jewellery special can also trap dust and moisture. Store each piece flat in its own lined box, away from humidity. Wipe gently with a soft, dry cloth after wearing and avoid perfume, water and chemical cleaners. For deep cleaning or loose stones, take the piece to a jeweller rather than soaking it at home. Our care guide covers the basics in more detail.

Temple jewellery is more than an accessory. It carries centuries of devotion, craft and celebration, and wearing it is a small way of keeping that story alive.

posts.title: Layering Necklaces: A Simple Guide for Every Neckline
posts.excerpt: How to combine chains and pendants so they look effortless rather than tangled, with lengths, spacing and neckline pairings that work every time.
posts.author: House of Jewelux Atelier
posts.authorBio: The design and care team at our Jaipur atelier, writing about the pieces we make and how to live with them.
posts.coverAlt: A woman wearing several fine layered necklaces with stacked rings and a bracelet
posts.html:
Layered necklaces look effortless when they work and messy when they do not. The difference is rarely about how expensive the pieces are; it is about length, spacing, weight and the neckline you are wearing. Once you understand a few simple rules, you can build layers from pieces you already own.

Start with lengths

Necklace lengths have common names, and knowing them makes layering much easier:

  • Collar or choker (about 35–40 cm): sits close around the neck
  • Princess (about 43–48 cm): rests on or just below the collarbone
  • Matinee (about 50–60 cm): falls to the top of the chest
  • Opera (about 70–85 cm): falls to the bust or below
  • Rope (over 85 cm): can be worn long or doubled

The easiest layered look uses three different lengths, each about 5 to 8 cm apart. That gap lets each piece be seen and stops them from twisting into each other.

The secret of good layering is space. Each chain needs its own lane.

Balance weight and detail

Think of your layers as a composition with one hero and two supporting pieces:

  1. A fine base chain close to the neck, plain or with a tiny charm.
  2. A middle layer with a little more presence, such as a slightly heavier chain or a small pendant.
  3. A statement layer at the longest length, carrying the main pendant or the most detail.

If every layer has a large pendant, they compete. If every layer is a plain fine chain, the look can disappear. One clear focal point keeps it intentional.

Match the neckline

Crew necks and high necklines

Wear layers over the fabric or keep them short and fine above it. Longer matinee and opera lengths work well over a plain knit or a fitted kurta.

V-necks

Follow the shape. Layers that form a soft V, with the longest pendant dropping towards the point of the neckline, look natural and lengthen the neck.

Scoop necks and off-shoulder

These are the easiest necklines for layering. Choose collar and princess lengths that sit on the skin, with a delicate pendant on the longest layer.

Shirts and collars

With an open collar, keep layers fine and close to the neck. With a buttoned shirt, a single longer chain worn over it can be enough.

Mixing metals and styles

Mixing metals is no longer a rule to avoid. Silver and gold tones can look modern together, especially when you repeat each tone at least twice, for example a gold chain, a silver chain and a pendant that has both. Mixing traditional and contemporary pieces also works: a small temple pendant on a fine chain can sit beautifully next to a minimal modern layer.

Keeping layers from tangling

Tangling is the most common complaint about layering. These habits help:

  • Choose chains with different link styles, which slide against each other less.
  • Use slightly different weights, with heavier chains at the longer lengths.
  • Put the longest necklace on first and the shortest last.
  • Consider a layering clasp or spacer, which keeps several chains separate at the back.
  • Take layers off one at a time and store each one fastened, in its own pouch.

Three easy combinations to try

  • Everyday: a fine collar chain, a princess-length chain with a tiny stone, and a matinee-length pendant.
  • Evening: a short sparkling chain, a medium plain chain, and a long chain with a bold drop.
  • Festive: a coin or temple pendant on the longest layer, balanced by two fine plain chains above it.

Final check in the mirror

Step back and look at the whole outfit. If your eye jumps between pieces, remove one. If the look feels flat, swap a plain chain for one with a pendant. Layering is personal, and the best combinations usually come from playing with what you already have. If you would like help choosing pieces that work together, our concierge is happy to suggest combinations.

posts.title: Polki, Kundan and Meenakari: Three Indian Techniques Explained
posts.excerpt: The differences between three of India's best-known jewellery techniques, how each one is made, how to recognise them, and how to care for them.
posts.author: House of Jewelux Atelier
posts.authorBio: The design and care team at our Jaipur atelier, writing about the pieces we make and how to live with them.
posts.coverAlt: A gold maang tikka set with coloured stones and a fringe of small gold drops

toc.text: Polki: diamonds in their natural form
Questions worth asking before you buy
Caring for polki, kundan and meenakari

posts.html:
Polki, kundan and meenakari are names you will hear in almost every conversation about traditional Indian jewellery. They are often mentioned together, and many pieces combine all three, but they describe different things. Polki is a kind of stone, kundan is a way of setting stones, and meenakari is the art of enamelling. Understanding the difference helps you appreciate what you are looking at and ask the right questions before you buy.

Polki: diamonds in their natural form

Polki refers to uncut diamonds. Instead of being cut into many reflective facets like a modern brilliant diamond, a polki stone keeps a flatter, more natural shape with only minimal shaping and polishing. The result is a softer, glowing sparkle rather than a bright flash.

Because each polki stone has its own shape, pieces are designed around the stones rather than the other way round. That is one reason why no two polki pieces are exactly alike.

What to look for

  • A flat or gently domed surface with a soft, mirror-like glow
  • Irregular outlines that follow the stone's natural shape
  • A foil backing in many traditional pieces, which reflects light back through the stone

Kundan: the art of setting

Kundan is a setting technique. The word refers to highly refined gold, which is worked into thin strips and pressed around the stone to hold it in place. Unlike claw or prong settings, kundan surrounds the stone with a smooth gold frame.

The technique has long been associated with the royal courts of Rajasthan and the Mughal period, and Jaipur and Bikaner remain known for it today. Kundan settings can hold polki, coloured stones or glass, which is why it is important to ask what kind of stone is set in a kundan piece.

Kundan describes how a stone is held. Polki describes what the stone is. A piece can be polki set in kundan, or kundan-set with other stones entirely.

Meenakari: colour in enamel

Meenakari is the art of decorating metal with coloured enamel. The craftsperson engraves small hollows into the metal, fills them with coloured enamel powder and fires the piece so the enamel melts and fuses. Colours are applied and fired one at a time, often starting with those that need the highest heat.

Jaipur is particularly known for meenakari, with its rich reds, greens and blues on a gold ground. Very often meenakari decorates the back of a kundan or polki piece, so the reverse is as beautiful as the front. Turn a traditional necklace over and you may find birds, flowers and vines in bright enamel.

How the three come together

A traditional bridal piece might use all three:

  1. A design is shaped in gold and the back is engraved.
  2. The back is enamelled in meenakari, colour by colour.
  3. The stones, often polki, are set on the front using the kundan technique.
  4. Pearls, drops and threads are added to finish the piece.

This layered process is why such pieces take time to make and why they are often handed down as heirlooms.

Questions worth asking before you buy

  • What kind of stones are set in the piece: uncut diamonds, coloured gemstones or glass?
  • What metal and purity is the setting?
  • Is the enamel hand-applied meenakari?
  • How should it be stored and cleaned?

A reputable jeweller will answer clearly, and the answers help you compare pieces fairly.

Caring for polki, kundan and meenakari

These pieces need gentle care:

  • Store flat in a lined box, separated from other jewellery, to protect enamel and settings.
  • Keep away from water, perfume and creams; moisture can affect foil backings.
  • Wipe with a soft, dry cloth after wearing. Do not soak or use ultrasonic cleaners.
  • Have settings checked by a jeweller if a stone feels loose.

Learning to recognise these three techniques changes how you look at Indian jewellery. Each piece becomes a record of several crafts working together, and a little understanding makes it even more rewarding to wear. For more on looking after traditional pieces, see our care guide.

posts.title: Gemstone Care: Keeping Emeralds, Rubies, Sapphires and Pearls at Their Best
posts.excerpt: Every gemstone has its own needs. A practical guide to cleaning, wearing and storing the stones you are most likely to own, and the mistakes that cause lasting damage.
posts.author: House of Jewelux Atelier
posts.authorBio: The design and care team at our Jaipur atelier, writing about the pieces we make and how to live with them.
posts.coverAlt: A pair of blue gemstone drop earrings resting on a large green leaf

toc.text: Hardness is not the whole story

posts.html:
Gemstones are often thought of as indestructible, but each one has its own strengths and weaknesses. Some are hard but brittle, some are soft, and some are sensitive to heat, light or chemicals. Knowing what you own is the first step to keeping it beautiful. This guide covers the stones you are most likely to find in a jewellery box, along with the general habits that protect all of them.

Hardness is not the whole story

Gem hardness is usually described on the Mohs scale, from 1 (very soft) to 10 (diamond). A higher number means the stone resists scratches better. But hardness does not measure toughness, which is resistance to chipping and breaking. A stone can be hard yet still crack if it is knocked at the wrong angle.

Treat every gemstone as if it could chip, even the hardest ones. Most damage happens in a moment: a knock against a door frame, a drop onto a tiled floor.

Stone by stone

Rubies and sapphires

Rubies and sapphires are both varieties of the mineral corundum, with a hardness of 9. They are among the most durable coloured stones for everyday wear. Warm water with a little mild soap and a soft brush is usually safe for untreated stones. Many rubies and sapphires are treated to improve colour or clarity, and some treatments are sensitive to heat or chemicals, so ask what treatment your stone has had before using anything stronger than soap and water.

Emeralds

Emeralds are hard (7.5 to 8) but they usually contain natural inclusions, which make them more fragile than their hardness suggests. Most emeralds are also treated with oils or resins to improve clarity. For these reasons:

  • avoid hot water, steam and ultrasonic cleaners
  • clean with a soft, damp cloth and dry immediately
  • avoid sudden temperature changes
  • take emerald rings off for any work with your hands

Diamonds

Diamonds are the hardest natural material, but they attract grease, which dulls their sparkle quickly. Soaking in warm soapy water and brushing gently behind the stone restores brightness. Diamonds can still chip along certain directions, so protect them from hard knocks.

Pearls

Pearls are organic and soft (around 2.5 to 4.5), and they react to acids, perfume, cosmetics and even sweat. They need the gentlest care of all:

  1. Put pearls on last, after perfume and make-up.
  2. Wipe them with a soft, slightly damp cloth after every wear.
  3. Never soak them; water can weaken the silk thread.
  4. Store them flat, never hanging, so the thread does not stretch.
  5. Have strung pearls restrung every few years if worn often.

Habits that protect every stone

Whatever the gemstone, the same everyday habits help:

  • Remove jewellery before cleaning, gardening, swimming or the gym.
  • Store pieces separately so harder stones cannot scratch softer ones.
  • Keep stones out of long, direct sunlight and away from heat.
  • Check settings regularly by gently feeling for movement.
  • Know which treatments your stones have had; it changes how they should be cleaned.

Mistakes that cause lasting damage

Most serious gemstone damage comes from a small number of mistakes:

  • Using ultrasonic or steam cleaners on emeralds, pearls, opals or treated stones.
  • Cleaning with bleach, ammonia or harsh household products.
  • Storing everything together in one pouch.
  • Wearing rings with large stones during sport or heavy work.
  • Ignoring a loose stone until it falls out.

When to visit a jeweller

A professional check every year or two is worthwhile, especially for rings and bracelets that are worn daily. A jeweller can tighten settings, clean safely, and spot early wear on clasps and prongs before a stone is lost. If you are unsure how to clean a particular piece, it is always safer to ask than to experiment.

Gemstones are meant to be worn and enjoyed. A little knowledge about the stones you own turns care into a simple routine, and keeps them looking their best for many years. Our care guide has more general advice, and our concierge can help with specific pieces.
